title: How to diagnose high CPU usage — thread dump (`jstack`), look for threads in RUNNABLE state doing heavy computation or infinite loops, or excessive GC (check GC logs)?
shortTitle: How do you diagnose high CPU usage?

s1_definition.profdef: Diagnosing high CPU in a Java process means identifying which threads are burning CPU and what code they are running. The standard technique is to find the operating-system threads consuming the most CPU, convert their native thread IDs to hexadecimal, take a thread dump with `jstack`, and match the hot native IDs to Java threads. Threads stuck in the RUNNABLE state doing heavy computation or spinning in an infinite loop are the usual culprits. The other major cause is excessive garbage collection, which you confirm by reading GC logs to see if GC threads are eating the CPU.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's branch where the air conditioning bill suddenly doubles because someone is working flat-out. To find who, you first check the meter to see which counter is drawing the most power (top shows the hottest threads). Then you take a snapshot of what every teller is doing at that instant (jstack thread dump) and match the power-hungry counter to the specific teller and the exact task on their desk. If a teller is stuck re-counting the same stack of notes forever, that is an infinite loop. But sometimes the whole branch is hot not because of a teller but because the cleaning crew is running non-stop — that is excessive garbage collection, which you confirm by checking the cleaning logs.
s1_definition.oneliner: Find the hottest threads with top, take a jstack dump, match the hot native thread IDs to Java stacks, and rule out excessive GC via the GC logs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Diagnosing high CPU in a Java process means identifying which threads are burning CPU and what code they are running. The standard technique is to find the operating-system threads consuming the most CPU, convert their native thread IDs to hexadecimal, take a thread dump with `jstack`, and match the hot native IDs to Java threads. Threads stuck in the RUNNABLE state doing heavy computation or spinning in an infinite loop are the usual culprits. The other major cause is excessive garbage collection, which you confirm by reading GC logs to see if GC threads are eating the CPU.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's branch where the air conditioning bill suddenly doubles because someone is working flat-out. To find who, you first check the meter to see which counter is drawing the most power (top shows the hottest threads). Then you take a snapshot of what every teller is doing at that instant (jstack thread dump) and match the power-hungry counter to the specific teller and the exact task on their desk. If a teller is stuck re-counting the same stack of notes forever, that is an infinite loop. But sometimes the whole branch is hot not because of a teller but because the cleaning crew is running non-stop — that is excessive garbage collection, which you confirm by checking the cleaning logs.

**One line to remember:** Find the hottest threads with top, take a jstack dump, match the hot native thread IDs to Java stacks, and rule out excessive GC via the GC logs.

sections.s2_technical:
The reliable method links operating-system CPU usage to a specific Java thread. On Linux you run `top -H -p <pid>` to show per-thread CPU for the Java process. You note the thread IDs (TIDs) burning the most CPU. Those are decimal native IDs. You convert each to hexadecimal, because a Java thread dump records the native id in hex under `nid=`. Then you take a thread dump with `jstack <pid>` and search for the matching `nid=0x...`. The stack trace at that thread tells you exactly which Java method is running hot.

A thread in the RUNNABLE state in the dump is actively using CPU (or ready to). If you see the same RUNNABLE stack across several dumps taken a few seconds apart, and it is deep inside a computation or a loop, that is your hotspot. A classic finding is an infinite or near-infinite loop — for example a `while` loop whose exit condition is never met, or a spin on a flag without a sleep. Another common finding is an unexpectedly expensive operation inside a hot path, like a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking or repeated string building.

The second major cause of high CPU is excessive garbage collection. If the application threads are not obviously hot but CPU is pinned, the GC threads may be the ones working. You confirm this by reading GC logs (`-Xlog:gc`): if GC is running almost continuously and total GC time is a large fraction of uptime, the CPU is going into collection, usually because the heap is too small, there is a leak, or allocation is far too high. In a thread dump, GC threads show as JVM-internal threads, and tools like JFR or `jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000` make the GC-bound situation obvious.

A senior nuance: take several thread dumps a few seconds apart rather than one, because a single dump is a snapshot that might catch a thread mid-normal-work. The hotspot is the stack that keeps appearing. Also distinguish user CPU (your code or GC computing) from system CPU (often heavy I/O or context switching). For deeper analysis, async-profiler's CPU flame graph pinpoints the hot method without the manual TID matching. And always profile under the real load that triggers the problem.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's fraud-check service pegged a CPU core at 100 percent in production, slowing every other request on the box. This is exactly the case where you find the hot thread and read its stack to see what it is computing.

Problem 2 — The hot thread turned out to be stuck in a retry loop that never backed off, spinning on a condition that was never true. This is exactly an infinite/spin loop in the RUNNABLE state, the classic high-CPU culprit.

Problem 3 — On another day, CPU was pinned but no application thread looked busy; the GC logs showed collection running nonstop. This is exactly the excessive-GC cause, diagnosed from GC logs rather than the thread dump.

Our mini-project builds a `HighCpuDemo` that starts a deliberately spinning fraud-check thread and a `ThreadDumpHelper` that captures the current thread stacks programmatically (like jstack) and highlights RUNNABLE threads so the reader can see how to spot the offender. A note shows how to correlate with top and GC logs.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
jvm-highcpu-demo/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/
            ├── HighCpuDemo.java           (main runnable demo)
            ├── FraudCheckWorker.java      (the spinning hot thread)
            └── ThreadDumpHelper.java      (captures + highlights RUNNABLE threads)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/jvm/*.java

# Run; the fraud-check-spinner thread will peg a CPU core
java -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.HighCpuDemo

# The REAL production procedure (Linux):
# 1) find the hot JVM pid and its hottest thread id (TID)
top -H -p <pid>                 # note the TID using most %CPU
# 2) convert that decimal TID to hex
printf '%x\n' <TID>             # e.g. 12345 -> 3039
# 3) take a thread dump and find the matching nid
jstack <pid> | grep -A 20 'nid=0x3039'   # shows the hot Java stack

# Rule out excessive GC as the CPU cause:
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000        # watch GC time %; or read -Xlog:gc output

# Easiest: CPU flame graph pinpoints the hot method directly
java -agentpath:/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so=start,event=cpu,file=/tmp/cpu.html \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.HighCpuDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a running JVM with one deliberately spinning fraud-check thread.

Step 1 — The FraudCheckWorker starts and enters a tight `while` loop that never blocks and never exits, so it uses a full CPU core continuously. This is the production symptom: a pegged core.

Step 2 — In a real incident you run `top -H -p <pid>` and see one thread consuming nearly 100 percent CPU. You record its decimal thread id.

Step 3 — You convert that decimal id to hexadecimal with `printf '%x'`, because thread dumps list the native id in hex under `nid=`.

Step 4 — You take a thread dump with `jstack <pid>` and search for the matching `nid=0x...`. The demo's ThreadDumpHelper does the Java-side equivalent: it lists every thread, highlights the RUNNABLE ones, and prints their accumulated CPU time and top stack frame.

Step 5 — You take a second dump a couple of seconds later. The `fraud-check-spinner` thread is RUNNABLE in both dumps with ever-growing CPU time, and its top frame is the spin loop. A thread that is RUNNABLE across multiple dumps in the same spot is the hotspot.

Step 6 — You also check `jstat -gcutil` or the GC logs. Here GC time is low, confirming the CPU is going into the application thread, not the collector. The fix is to add a proper wait or backoff instead of busy-spinning.

Final output:

```
2026-10-31 23:22:00 [INFO] Started fraud-check worker (it will spin and burn a CPU core)
2026-10-31 23:22:02 [INFO] ==== Dump #1 (RUNNABLE threads first) ====
2026-10-31 23:22:02 [WARNING] RUNNABLE 'fraud-check-spinner' cpu=1990ms top=com.bank.jvm.FraudCheckWorker.run(FraudCheckWorker.java)
2026-10-31 23:22:04 [INFO] ==== Dump #2 (RUNNABLE threads first) ====
2026-10-31 23:22:04 [WARNING] RUNNABLE 'fraud-check-spinner' cpu=3980ms top=com.bank.jvm.FraudCheckWorker.run(FraudCheckWorker.java)
2026-10-31 23:22:04 [INFO] Worker stopped; the thread that appeared RUNNABLE in BOTH dumps was the hotspot
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  High CPU observed on the box
    │
    ▼
  top -H -p <pid>  → hottest TID (decimal)
    │ printf '%x' TID
    ▼
  jstack <pid> | grep nid=0x<hex>
    │
    ├─ thread RUNNABLE in loop/compute (same across 2 dumps)
    │     │ → APPLICATION hotspot (spin loop / expensive op)
    │     ▼ FIX: add backoff/wait, optimize the hot method
    │
    └─ no app thread hot, but CPU pinned
          │ jstat -gcutil / -Xlog:gc → GC time high?
          ▼ → EXCESSIVE GC (small heap / leak / high alloc)
            FIX: size heap, fix leak, reduce allocation

  Demo equivalent: ThreadDumpHelper.dumpRunnable() ×2
  → 'fraud-check-spinner' RUNNABLE in both, cpu rising → hotspot
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Thread Dump Inspection Design ═══

  ┌─ SOLID Applied ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: FraudCheckWorker does work; ThreadDumpHelper only  │
  │     inspects thread state — one job each               │
  │  D: ThreadDumpHelper depends on ThreadMXBean           │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  State Diagram: Thread States in a Dump
  [RUNNABLE] ← CPU burner (loop/compute)  ← look HERE for high CPU
  [BLOCKED]  ← waiting for a lock          ← look here for deadlock/contention
  [WAITING / TIMED_WAITING] ← parked/sleeping ← usually NOT the CPU cause

  ┌──────────────────────┐ reads ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │   ThreadDumpHelper   │──────▶│ ThreadMXBean               │
  │ + dumpRunnable(label)│       │ dumpAllThreads()           │
  │                      │       │ getThreadCpuTime(id)       │
  └──────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────┐ implements ┌──────────────────┐
  │  FraudCheckWorker    │───────────▶│   Runnable       │
  │ - running, condition │            └──────────────────┘
  │ + run() {spin loop}  │ (Caution) busy-spin
  └──────────────────────┘

  Call Chain:
  1. start fraud-check-spinner        [enters tight loop → 100% core]
  2. dumpRunnable("Dump #1")          [RUNNABLE + cpu time]
  3. sleep, dumpRunnable("Dump #2")   [SAME thread RUNNABLE, cpu rising]
  4. persistent RUNNABLE = hotspot
  5. check GC time (rule out GC)      [low → app hotspot confirmed]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When a Java process pegs the CPU, I do not guess; I link the operating system's view of CPU to a specific Java thread and the exact line it is running. On Linux I run top with the per-thread flag on the process id to see which thread is burning the most CPU, I note that thread's decimal id, and I convert it to hexadecimal, because a Java thread dump records the native id in hex. Then I take a thread dump with jstack and search for that hex id, and the stack trace right there tells me precisely which method is hot. A thread that is in the RUNNABLE state and sitting in the same deep computation or loop across two dumps taken a few seconds apart is my hotspot, and the classic finding is an infinite or spinning loop with no backoff, or an unexpectedly expensive operation like a regex with catastrophic backtracking.

The second thing I always check is whether the CPU is actually going into garbage collection rather than my own code. If no application thread looks busy but the CPU is still pinned, the GC threads are probably the ones working. I confirm that by reading the GC logs or running jstat to watch the GC time percentage, and if GC is running almost continuously the real problem is a heap that is too small, a memory leak, or an allocation rate that is far too high. I take several dumps rather than one, because a single snapshot can mislead, and for the fastest answer I use an async-profiler CPU flame graph, where the widest box is immediately the hot method with no manual id matching.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this procedure solved two very different incidents. In one, our fraud-check service pinned a CPU core, and the thread dump showed a thread stuck RUNNABLE in a retry loop that spun on a condition that was never true with no backoff, so we fixed it by adding a proper wait and bounded retries. In another, the CPU was pinned but no application thread looked busy, and the GC logs revealed collection running nonstop because the heap was undersized for the load, so the fix was sizing the heap correctly rather than touching any application code. Knowing to separate an application hotspot from a GC-bound situation is what lets me fix the right thing fast under production pressure.

---

keyPoints: top -H -p PID: find the thread consuming CPU
Convert thread ID to hex: printf "%x" TID
jstack PID: thread dump — find the hex TID in the output
Common causes: infinite loop, busy-wait, excessive GC, regex backtracking
JFR CPU profiling shows exactly which methods consume the most CPU
